questions.prompt: Your app follows the Now in Android layout, where each feature is split into `:feature:x:api` and `:feature:x:impl`. `:feature:interests:impl` must open the Topic screen owned by the topic feature. Which dependency keeps the features decoupled?

choices.text: `:feature:interests:impl` depends on `:feature:topic:impl` so it can call the Topic screen composable directly
`:feature:topic:impl` depends on `:feature:interests:impl` and registers a callback
`:feature:interests:impl` depends on `:feature:topic:api`, which exposes the Topic navigation key or navigator
Both features depend on `:app`, which exposes the Topic screen composable

sources.claim: A feature's impl should only depend on another feature's api module; :topic:api exposes a navigator that :interests:impl uses to navigate to the TopicScreen.
sources.title: Now in Android: Modularization learning journey

sources.claim: Feature modules should not depend directly on each other; communication goes through a mediator or shared modules to keep coupling low.
sources.title: Common modularization patterns

questions.explanation: In Now in Android a feature's `api` module exposes only navigation keys, and a feature's `impl` may depend only on another feature's `api`. Navigating through `:feature:topic:api` means the Topic UI can change without recompiling Interests. Depending on the other feature's `impl` (the tempting choice) couples the two features' internals and builds together.

questions.prompt: A module `:core:data` changes from `api(project(":core:network"))` to `implementation(project(":core:network"))`. Which build benefit follows directly from that change?

choices.text: Modules depending only on `:core:data` no longer recompile when `:core:network` changes, since it's off their compile classpath
`:core:network` is no longer packaged into the APK at all unless some other module in the graph also declares a direct or transitive dependency on it
Gradle can now skip the configuration phase entirely for `:core:network` on every subsequent build, because `implementation` enables the configuration cache
R8 can now remove `:core:network`'s classes from the final APK entirely, because `implementation` dependencies are excluded from reachability analysis

sources.claim: implementation dependencies do not leak into consumers' compile classpath, giving faster compilation and fewer recompilations because consumers need not be recompiled when implementation dependencies change.
sources.title: The Java Library Plugin

sources.claim: Prefer implementation over api; api exposes transitive dependencies to the consumers of your module.
sources.title: Common modularization patterns

questions.explanation: `implementation` dependencies do not leak onto consumers' compile classpath, so consumers are not recompiled when those dependencies change, and the smaller classpath compiles faster. The dependency is still present at runtime and in the APK, so the packaging and R8 choices are wrong; skipping configuration is what the configuration cache does, not a dependency configuration.

questions.prompt: After a modularization push, a 40-screen app has 350 Gradle modules, many holding one or two classes. Builds got slower and every new feature needs several boilerplate build files. Which pitfall does the Android modularization guide name for this?

choices.text: Too coarse-grained: modules are still too large and tightly coupled internally to benefit from parallel builds or independent recompilation
Too complex: the guide says modularization is never worthwhile for apps with fewer than 100 screens or without a dedicated build team
Missing an `api`/`impl` split: every module, no matter how small, should still be split into a separate `api` and `impl` pair
Too fine-grained: many small modules add build complexity and boilerplate that can outweigh the benefits

sources.claim: The guide lists pitfalls: too fine-grained (overhead in build complexity and boilerplate), too coarse-grained, and too complex for small projects.
sources.title: Guide to Android app modularization

questions.explanation: The guide lists three granularity pitfalls. Very many tiny modules is the too-fine-grained one: each module adds build configuration and overhead, which can cancel the gains. 'Too coarse' is the opposite problem, and 'too complex' refers to small projects that never reach the growth threshold. Splitting every module into `api`/`impl` would make the problem worse.

questions.prompt: Using the Now in Android module rules, which dependency is a violation?

choices.text: `:feature:bookmarks:impl` depends on `:feature:topic:api`
`:core:ui` depends on `:feature:settings:impl`
`:core:data` depends on `:core:network`
`:app` depends on `:feature:bookmarks:impl`

sources.claim: Core modules can depend on other core modules, but they shouldn't depend on feature nor app modules; a feature's impl should only depend on another feature's api module.
sources.title: Now in Android: Modularization learning journey

sources.claim: App modules depend on feature modules and usually provide root navigation.
sources.title: Common modularization patterns

questions.explanation: Core modules may depend on other core modules but never on feature or app modules; a core module depending on a feature inverts the layering and makes cycles likely. A feature `impl` depending on another feature's `api`, core depending on core, and the app module wiring feature implementations together are all allowed.

questions.prompt: `:feature:profile:impl` uses Retrofit only in internal classes, yet its build file says `api(libs.retrofit)`. What is the most important consequence for the rest of the codebase?

choices.text: Retrofit is downloaded twice: once for the `api` configuration and once again for `implementation`, doubling the dependency resolution time
Retrofit is excluded from the release build entirely, because `api` dependencies are only ever placed on the compile classpath, never packaged
Retrofit leaks onto every consumer's compile classpath, so callers can accidentally use it and get recompiled when it changes
Nothing observable changes at build or runtime; `api` and `implementation` only affect metadata published to a Maven repository

sources.claim: Dependencies in the api configuration are transitively exposed to consumers and appear on their compile classpath; implementation dependencies do not leak.
sources.title: The Java Library Plugin

sources.claim: The public interface of a module should be minimal and should not leak implementation details; prefer implementation over api.
sources.title: Common modularization patterns

questions.explanation: `api` dependencies are exposed transitively and appear on consumers' compile classpath. Consumers can start depending on Retrofit by accident, which breaks encapsulation, and they must recompile when it changes. `api` is not compile-only, and the difference matters for every build, not just publishing.

questions.prompt: You are splitting a checkout feature out of a large single-module app. Describe the module structure and the dependency rules you would put in place so the feature stays independent, including how other features reach it.

sources.claim: Feature api modules expose navigation keys and impl modules contain feature logic and UI; an impl depends only on another feature's api; core modules don't depend on feature or app modules.
sources.title: Now in Android: Modularization learning journey

sources.claim: You shouldn't pass objects as navigation arguments; use simple ids that features use to load resources from the data layer.
sources.title: Common modularization patterns

questions.explanation: A senior answer names concrete, enforceable rules (who may depend on whom) rather than 'keep modules decoupled', and explains why each rule matters: API-only dependencies keep recompilation local, and one-way layering prevents cycles.

model_answer.summary: Split checkout into a small API module (navigation keys, public models or interfaces) and an implementation module (UI, ViewModels, internal logic). Other features depend only on the API; the app module wires implementations and owns root navigation; core modules never depend on features.
key_points: Checkout gets an `api` module exposing only navigation keys or contracts and an `impl` module with UI, ViewModels and internals marked `internal`
Other feature `impl` modules may depend on `:feature:checkout:api` only, never on its `impl`; feature `api` modules depend on no other feature
Core modules (data, network, ui) never depend on feature or app modules, which keeps the graph acyclic
The app module depends on the `impl` modules, wires them together (DI) and owns root navigation
Features pass simple IDs as navigation arguments and load data from a shared data module rather than passing objects

questions.prompt: A teammate wants to navigate from the book-details feature to checkout by passing the whole `Book` object as a navigation argument, and proposes making `:feature:checkout` depend on `:feature:bookdetails` to share the `Book` class. Critique the proposal and give a better design.

sources.claim: Feature modules should not depend on each other; the mediator is the module that owns the navigation graph (usually an app module), and features pass simple ids instead of objects.
sources.title: Common modularization patterns

sources.claim: Both feature modules depending on the same data module minimizes the data the mediator must forward and keeps coupling low.
sources.title: Common modularization patterns

questions.explanation: The official guidance is explicit: features shouldn't depend on each other, and navigation arguments should be IDs. A strong answer also notes that shared models belong in a data or model module, not in either feature.

model_answer.summary: Don't couple two feature modules or pass objects as navigation arguments. Let a mediator (the module that owns navigation, usually the app module) route between features, pass the book ID, and have both features depend on a shared data module that loads the `Book`.
key_points: A direct feature-to-feature dependency raises coupling and makes cycles and cross-team build impact likely
Navigation should go through a mediator, usually the app module that owns the navigation graph, or through the target feature's API module
Pass a primitive ID (the book ID) rather than an object; objects in navigation arguments get stale and couple the features' models
Both features depend on the same data module, which exposes a repository to load the book by ID

questions.prompt: Your director asks whether modularizing a 200k-line single-module app is worth it and how you would prove it. Explain the benefits you would expect, the risks, and what you would measure before and after.

sources.claim: Gradle functionalities such as incremental build, build cache or parallel build can leverage modularity to improve build performance; pitfalls include too fine-grained and too coarse-grained modules.
sources.title: Guide to Android app modularization

sources.claim: Parallel builds can significantly improve build times, but the impact depends on the project's structure and inter-subproject dependencies; build scans and profile reports identify bottlenecks.
sources.title: Improve the Performance of Gradle Builds

questions.explanation: Senior answers treat modularization as an investment with a measurable return, and they know the build win comes from specific Gradle mechanisms that need a loosely coupled graph. Saying 'modules make builds faster' without that condition is the junior answer.

model_answer.summary: Modularization pays off through visibility control, ownership, testability and build performance (incremental builds, build cache and parallel execution work per module), but only with the right granularity. Measure build times on representative scenarios and track ownership and coupling, and avoid too-fine or too-coarse modules.
key_points: Expected benefits: strict visibility (`internal`), clear team ownership per module, isolated testing, and Play Feature Delivery options
Build-time gains come from Gradle features that exploit modules: incremental builds, the build cache and parallel execution of decoupled modules
Risks: too fine-grained modules add configuration overhead and boilerplate; too coarse-grained ones recreate the monolith
Measure first: profile clean and incremental builds for common changes (Build Analyzer or build scans), then compare after the split
Parallel speedup depends on how coupled the modules are, so also track the dependency graph (depth, and cycles avoided)

questions.prompt: With `org.gradle.configuration-cache=true`, what does Gradle reuse on a cache hit?

choices.text: The compiled outputs of tasks whose inputs haven't changed, including outputs fetched from other machines through a shared remote build cache
The result of the configuration phase (the task graph and each task's state), skipping build-script and plugin re-evaluation
The downloaded dependency JARs and their transitive metadata, so a cache hit needs no network access even on a completely clean checkout
The Gradle daemon JVM process itself, including its warmed-up classes, so daemon startup and JIT warm-up are both skipped entirely

sources.claim: The configuration cache stores the result of the configuration phase (the task graph, task state and dependency information); on a hit the configuration phase is skipped and build scripts and plugins are not re-evaluated.
sources.title: Configuration Cache

sources.claim: The build cache stores task outputs and lets builds fetch them when inputs have not changed, locally or from a remote cache.
sources.title: Build Cache

questions.explanation: The configuration cache stores the output of the configuration phase: the task graph and task state. On a hit, settings and build scripts and plugins are not evaluated again. Reusing task outputs (the tempting choice) is the build cache, a separate feature enabled with `org.gradle.caching`.

questions.prompt: A team adds `gradle/libs.versions.toml` and expects every module to now use the same `compileSdk`, Kotlin JVM target and lint settings. Nothing changes. Why?

choices.text: The catalog must be named exactly `versions.toml` (not `libs.versions.toml`) and placed at the project root for Gradle to auto-apply it
The catalog also needs a `[bundles]` section defined before any module can automatically pick up shared `compileSdk`, Kotlin and lint settings from it
A version catalog only declares dependency and plugin coordinates and versions; shared configuration needs a convention plugin to apply it
The catalog applies its settings only after a full Gradle sync completes with the configuration cache disabled in `gradle.properties`

sources.claim: The catalog in gradle/libs.versions.toml has [versions], [libraries] and [plugins] sections; modules reference entries such as libs.androidx.ktx, and convention plugins are applied with id rather than alias.
sources.title: Migrate your build to version catalogs

sources.claim: Convention plugins encapsulate shared build configuration and are applied by subprojects that need it.
sources.title: Sharing Build Logic between Subprojects

questions.explanation: A version catalog is declarative: it gives modules type-safe aliases such as `libs.androidx.ktx` but applies nothing. Shared settings such as `compileSdk` belong in convention plugins that each module applies with `id(...)`. `libs.versions.toml` is the default name Gradle looks for, and `[bundles]` only groups libraries.

questions.prompt: Why is kapt slower than KSP for a processor like Room?

choices.text: kapt runs annotation processors in a completely separate long-lived JVM process with no incremental caching, unlike KSP which reuses the Kotlin compiler daemon
kapt processes the Java bytecode produced after Kotlin compilation finishes, so the module effectively has to be compiled twice for every build
KSP skips type checking of the annotated code entirely and trusts the generated sources, while kapt fully type-checks before generating anything
kapt must generate Java stubs from Kotlin sources for annotation processors to read; that step is expensive, while KSP reads Kotlin directly

sources.claim: kapt generates Java stubs from Kotlin files for processors to read, which is expensive; KSP analyzes Kotlin code directly and is up to 2x faster. kapt is in maintenance mode.
sources.title: Migrate from kapt to KSP

questions.explanation: kapt makes Java annotation processors work with Kotlin by generating Java stubs, and that step is a large part of its cost. KSP reads Kotlin symbols directly and is up to 2x faster. kapt does not run on bytecode, and KSP does not skip type information; it understands Kotlin constructs better.

questions.prompt: In `:core:database` you moved Room from kapt to KSP, but one legacy annotation processor there still has no KSP support and stays on kapt. Build time for the module barely improved. What explains this?

choices.text: While any kapt processor remains, kapt still generates stubs for the module, so most of the gain arrives only once kapt is fully removed
KSP and kapt cannot coexist in the same module at all; Gradle detects the conflict and silently falls back to running Room through kapt instead
KSP only speeds up clean builds; for incremental builds its performance is identical to kapt because both regenerate all stubs each time
Room's KSP processor is measurably slower than its kapt counterpart, because Room's code generation logic itself hasn't been ported to KSP

sources.claim: You can run kapt and KSP alongside each other while migrating, but if a module has any kapt processors remaining, stubs are still generated, so most of the improvement occurs only when all kapt usages are removed from the module.
sources.title: Migrate from kapt to KSP

questions.explanation: The migration guide says kapt and KSP can run side by side, but stubs are still generated in any module with a kapt processor left, so most of the improvement appears only when kapt is gone from the module. A practical fix is to move the legacy processor's code into its own module. They can coexist, so the 'silent fallback' choice is wrong.

questions.prompt: An app declares `flavorDimensions += listOf("api", "mode")` with three flavors in `api`, two in `mode`, and the `debug` and `release` build types. How many build variants does Gradle create, before any filtering?

sources.claim: The number of build variants equals the product of the number of flavors in each flavor dimension and the number of build types; 3 api flavors x 2 mode flavors x 2 build types gives 12.
sources.title: Configure build variants

questions.explanation: The number of variants is the product of the number of flavors in each dimension and the number of build types: 3 x 2 x 2 = 12. Adding the counts together (7) is the common mistake. Unwanted combinations can be disabled with `androidComponents.beforeVariants`.

questions.prompt: CI builds for a 60-module Android app take 14 minutes and local incremental builds feel slow. Walk through how you would diagnose the problem and which Gradle and Android settings you would change, and why each one helps.

sources.claim: Enable the configuration cache, migrate from kapt to KSP, avoid dynamic version numbers, raise the JVM heap if GC exceeds 15% of build time, and use the Build Analyzer to find bottlenecks.
sources.title: Optimize your build speed

sources.claim: The configuration cache stores the configuration phase result, while the build cache stores task outputs and intermediate artifacts.
sources.title: Configuration Cache

questions.explanation: The key senior distinction is between the two caches: the configuration cache removes configuration time, the build cache removes task execution time. Candidates who say 'turn on caching' without saying which, or who skip measurement, give a weaker answer.

model_answer.summary: Measure first (Build Analyzer, build scans), then use the configuration cache to skip configuration, the build cache (shared remotely with CI) to reuse task outputs, and parallel execution for decoupled modules. Remove kapt in favour of KSP, avoid dynamic versions, and size the JVM heap.
key_points: Profile before changing anything: Build Analyzer or build scans to see whether configuration, compilation or annotation processing dominates
The configuration cache skips the configuration phase on a hit; the build cache reuses task outputs by inputs, and a remote cache shares them between CI and developers
`org.gradle.parallel=true` runs decoupled modules at the same time; its benefit depends on how coupled the module graph is
Replace kapt with KSP where processors support it, since kapt's stub generation is expensive
Avoid dynamic dependency versions (`2.+`) and increase `org.gradle.jvmargs` if garbage collection takes a large share of build time

questions.prompt: Twenty module build scripts copy the same Android, Kotlin and Compose configuration. Design how you would centralize build logic, and compare convention plugins in an included `build-logic` build with `buildSrc` and with `subprojects {}` blocks.

sources.claim: Avoid subprojects {} and allprojects {} because logic can be injected into a subproject in a way that isn't obvious; changes to code in buildSrc invalidate the configuration phase and require re-execution of all tasks.
sources.title: Sharing Build Logic between Subprojects

sources.claim: Use alias for plugins from the version catalog and id for plugins that don't come from it, such as convention plugins.
sources.title: Migrate your build to version catalogs

questions.explanation: Strong answers separate 'what versions' (catalog) from 'how a module is configured' (convention plugins) and justify the included-build choice with the `buildSrc` invalidation cost. This is how Now in Android organizes `build-logic`.

model_answer.summary: Put versions in a version catalog and shared configuration in convention plugins, ideally in an included `build-logic` build, applied explicitly by each module. Avoid `subprojects {}` or `allprojects {}` injection, and know that changes in `buildSrc` invalidate configuration and rerun tasks.
key_points: A version catalog (`libs.versions.toml`) holds coordinates and versions; it does not apply configuration by itself
Convention plugins (such as `android-library`, `android-compose`, `jvm-library`) hold the shared settings and each module applies them with `id(...)`
`subprojects {}` and `allprojects {}` inject logic in ways that aren't visible from a module's own build script, so behaviour is hard to follow
`buildSrc` is automatic, but any change to it invalidates configuration and reruns all tasks; an included build is a standalone project that is more flexible for large builds
Measure build time before and after, and keep plugins compatible with the configuration cache

questions.prompt: Product wants free and paid editions, each able to point at a staging or production backend, with debug and release builds of the same edition installable side by side on one device. Design the variant setup and say how you would keep the variant count under control.

sources.claim: Gradle combines one flavor from each dimension with a build type; the count is the product. Build type suffix is applied after the flavor's, giving com.example.myapp.free.debug so debug and release can coexist.
sources.title: Configure build variants

sources.claim: Unwanted variants can be disabled with androidComponents.beforeVariants; source set priority is build variant, build type, product flavor, then main.
sources.title: Configure build variants

questions.explanation: Senior candidates think about the combinatorial cost: every variant multiplies build, test and CI work, so they filter variants rather than letting them grow. Knowing the suffix ordering and source-set precedence shows real experience.

model_answer.summary: Use two flavor dimensions (edition: free/paid; environment: staging/prod) plus the debug and release build types, which gives 2x2x2 = 8 variants. Use `applicationIdSuffix` so variants install side by side, `beforeVariants` to disable combinations nobody ships, and variant source sets for per-variant code.
key_points: Two flavor dimensions, `edition` (free, paid) and `environment` (staging, prod), combined with build types; variant count is the product (2x2x2 = 8)
`applicationIdSuffix` on flavors and build types (for example `.free` + `.debug` = `com.example.app.free.debug`) lets builds coexist, because no two apps can share an application ID
Disable unused combinations (such as `release` with `staging`) with `androidComponents.beforeVariants { enable = false }` to cut build and CI cost
Source set precedence: build variant > build type > flavor > `main`, so put per-environment config (base URLs) in the flavor source sets or `buildConfigField`s

questions.prompt: After enabling R8, the release build crashes with `ClassNotFoundException` for a class that a JSON library instantiates by reflection. Debug builds work. What is the best fix?

choices.text: Add `-keep class com.example.** { *; }` so nothing in the app is removed or renamed
Set `isMinifyEnabled = false` for release, since R8 is unsafe with reflection
Add a narrowly scoped keep rule for the classes and members accessed by reflection
Add `-dontwarn` for the class so R8 stops reporting it

sources.claim: R8 can't identify classes, fields or methods accessed with reflection and may rename or remove them, leading to ClassNotFoundException; narrowly scoped keep rules allow maximum optimization.
sources.title: About keep rules

sources.claim: The most common cause of crashes after R8 optimization is broken reflection (ClassNotFoundException, NoSuchMethodException and similar); the solution is to add a keep rule.
sources.title: Troubleshoot optimization

questions.explanation: R8 can't see reflective access, so it may rename or remove those classes, which produces `ClassNotFoundException` at runtime. The documented fix is a keep rule, as specific as possible so the rest of the app is still optimized. A package-wide `-keep` works but gives up most of R8's benefit; disabling minification throws away all of it; `-dontwarn` only silences build warnings and does nothing for a runtime crash.

questions.prompt: Your own crash reporter shows obfuscated stack traces (`a.b.c`) for release 5.3.0, which you built two weeks ago. Since then the team has built release candidates many times. What do you need to deobfuscate the 5.3.0 traces?

choices.text: The `mapping.txt` from the current build, since R8 always produces the exact same stable class and member mapping regardless of which commit is built
The `mapping.txt` from the exact 5.3.0 build, used with `retrace`; mapping files are overwritten every build, so each release must be archived
Only the source code checked out at the 5.3.0 git tag; the `retrace` tool recompiles it locally and recomputes the original R8 mapping from scratch
Nothing extra is needed; obfuscated names can be reversed directly from the APK's DEX file using any standard bytecode disassembler

sources.claim: Use the retrace tool with mapping.txt to deobfuscate stack traces; the mapping file is overwritten every time you build, so you must save a copy each time you publish a release.
sources.title: Troubleshoot optimization

questions.explanation: `retrace` maps obfuscated names back using the mapping file from the build that produced the binary. Android Studio writes it to `build/outputs/mapping/` and overwrites it on every build, so you must save a copy for each release. A mapping from a different build does not match, and obfuscation can't be reversed from the binary alone.

questions.prompt: What does uploading an Android App Bundle (`.aab`) instead of a universal APK change about what users download?

choices.text: Play generates and signs optimized APKs per device configuration, so a device downloads only the ABI, density and language resources it needs
The bundle itself is installed directly on devices and unpacked into a running APK by the Play Store app the first time it launches
The bundle format simply compresses resources better than a universal APK, but every device still receives every ABI, density and language
Users always download a small stub APK first, and every other part of the app streams in on demand regardless of what the developer configures

sources.claim: An app bundle defers APK generation and signing to Google Play, which generates optimized APKs for each device configuration so only the needed code and resources are downloaded.
sources.title: About Android App Bundles

sources.claim: From August 2021, new apps are required to publish with the Android App Bundle on Google Play.
sources.title: About Android App Bundles

questions.explanation: An app bundle is a publishing format; Play uses it to generate and serve device-specific APKs through configuration splits by ABI, screen density and language, and Play signs them (which requires Play App Signing). Devices never install the `.aab` itself, and on-demand downloads apply only to modules you configure that way.

questions.prompt: Your R8 output is much larger than expected, and you suspect some rule is keeping far more code than needed. Which tools help you find out why?

choices.text: `-dontobfuscate`, which disables renaming and prints every kept class alongside its original, unobfuscated name in the output mapping
Disabling full mode with `android.enableR8.fullMode=false`, rebuilding, and comparing the resulting APK sizes to isolate which rules changed
Reading `mapping.txt`, which lists, next to each class, the exact keep rule and source library responsible for retaining it
`-whyareyoukeeping` for a class or member, plus `configuration.txt`, which lists every merged rule including ones from libraries

sources.claim: configuration.txt contains all merged rules from every library and module used to configure R8; -whyareyoukeeping outputs a path from the kept code to an entry point.
sources.title: Troubleshoot optimization

questions.explanation: `-whyareyoukeeping` prints the path from the kept item to an entry point, and `build/outputs/mapping/configuration.txt` contains the merged rules from every library and module, which is where broad library rules and global options are found. `mapping.txt` maps names, not reasons, and turning off full mode only reduces optimization.

questions.prompt: You move a rarely used 'sell an item' flow into an on-demand Play Feature Delivery module. Which statement about that module is correct?

choices.text: The base `:app` module declares a dependency on the feature module, exactly as it would on any other ordinary library module in the project
The feature module declares its own `signingConfig`, `versionCode` and `versionName`, all independent of whatever the base module specifies
The feature module depends on the base `:app` module, and shouldn't declare `android:exported="true"` activities since it may not be installed yet
On-demand modules work on every Android version the app supports, including devices as old as API 19 (Android KitKat), with absolutely no extra runtime requirement at all

sources.claim: The feature module's build.gradle declares a dependency on the base module ':app' and omits signing configurations, minifyEnabled, versionCode and versionName.
sources.title: Overview of Play Feature Delivery

sources.claim: Feature modules should not specify activities with android:exported set to true, and only devices running Android 5.0 (API 21) and higher support on-demand features.
sources.title: Overview of Play Feature Delivery

questions.explanation: Feature modules reverse the usual direction: they depend on `:app`. They omit signing configs, `minifyEnabled` and version codes, which are inherited from the base. Exported activities are discouraged because the module might not be installed yet. On-demand install needs Android 5.0 (API 21) or higher.

questions.prompt: You enable R8 (full mode, the default in recent AGP) for release. QA reports three problems: a crash in JSON parsing, a JNI call that fails with `NoSuchMethodError`, and a feature that silently stops working in release only. How do you diagnose and fix these without giving up most of R8's benefit?

sources.claim: R8 can't identify reflective lookups or JNI calls based on dynamic string lookups, so its optimizations might break that code; keep rules should be as specific as possible.
sources.title: About keep rules

sources.claim: You should always enable optimization for the release build; R8 performs shrinking, optimizations such as inlining and class merging, and obfuscation, and full mode is enabled by default.
sources.title: Enable app optimization

questions.explanation: Senior answers explain why R8 breaks these cases (static reachability analysis can't see dynamic lookups) and refuse the easy fix of disabling R8 or keeping whole packages, because R8 improves startup, memory use and size.

model_answer.summary: All three point to R8 removing or renaming code it cannot see being used (reflection, JNI string lookups). Reproduce on a release build, retrace the stack traces with the build's mapping file, and add narrowly scoped keep rules (or use library-provided consumer rules), then check the result with the R8 diagnostics.
key_points: R8 can't see reflection (`Class.forName`, `getDeclaredMethod`, reflective serializers) or JNI's string-based method lookups, so it may rename or remove those members
Retrace the crashes with the `mapping.txt` from that exact build to find the real class and member
Add keep rules that are as specific as possible (just the model classes or native methods), not package-wide `-keep ... { *; }`
Use `configuration.txt` and `-whyareyoukeeping` to audit the merged rules, including broad rules from libraries
Test release (minified) builds in CI or pre-release, since the problems only appear there

questions.prompt: Design how your team makes sure every production crash and ANR from an R8-optimized build can be deobfuscated, both in Play Console and in a third-party crash reporter.

questions.prompt: Your open-source app's GitHub Actions workflow runs on `pull_request`. A PR from a fork fails at the step that decodes the upload keystore from `secrets.UPLOAD_KEYSTORE_BASE64`. Why?

choices.text: Base64-encoded secrets aren't supported by GitHub Actions at all; binary secrets must instead be committed to the repository pre-encrypted
Secrets are redacted in logs, and for that reason GitHub also clears the decoded value from the environment before the step actually runs
The keystore file is larger than GitHub's 1 KB per-secret size limit, so the encoding step silently truncates it before the step can read it
Except for `GITHUB_TOKEN`, secrets aren't passed to the runner for forked-repository workflows, and that token is read-only there

sources.claim: With the exception of GITHUB_TOKEN, secrets are not passed to the runner when a workflow is triggered from a forked repository; small binary blobs can be stored as Base64 secrets up to 48 KB.
sources.title: Using secrets in GitHub Actions

sources.claim: The GITHUB_TOKEN has read-only permissions in pull requests from forked repositories.
sources.title: Events that trigger workflows

questions.explanation: GitHub doesn't give secrets to workflows triggered from forks, so untrusted PR code can't read them. That's why PR builds should build, test and lint without signing, and signing belongs in a trusted job such as a push to `main`. Base64 is the documented way to store small binary files, masking affects log output only, and the limit is 48 KB.

questions.prompt: To let fork PRs sign builds, a teammate switches the workflow to `pull_request_target` and checks out the PR's head commit before running `./gradlew assembleRelease`. What is the main risk?

choices.text: `pull_request_target` runs with the base repository's permissions, so executing untrusted PR code there can expose secrets or poison caches
`pull_request_target` doesn't support Gradle-based workflows at all, so `assembleRelease` silently fails to resolve the Android Gradle plugin
The build always uses the base branch's checked-out code by default, so the actual PR changes are never compiled or really tested at all
There is no real risk here, because GitHub automatically masks any secret value that appears anywhere in the workflow's console log output

sources.claim: Running untrusted code on the pull_request_target trigger may lead to security vulnerabilities including cache poisoning and granting unintended access to write privileges or secrets.
sources.title: Events that trigger workflows

questions.explanation: `pull_request_target` runs with the base repository's privileges. Checking out and executing fork code there lets a malicious Gradle script read secrets or push with write access; GitHub warns about cache poisoning and secret access. Masking logs doesn't stop code from sending a secret elsewhere.

questions.prompt: Your app uses Play App Signing. A laptop holding the upload keystore is stolen. What is the situation?

choices.text: The app is lost entirely: current policy requires you to publish a completely unrelated new app listing under a brand-new package name and start over from zero
You can ask Google to reset the upload key with a new certificate; the app signing key, held by Google, is unaffected and keeps signing user APKs
Nothing needs to happen at all, because once Play App Signing is enabled the upload key no longer plays any role in the release process
You must immediately rotate the app signing key yourself, an action which silently uninstalls the app for every existing user overnight

sources.claim: You use the upload key to sign your app bundle before uploading; Google uses the app signing key to sign APKs delivered to users. If you lose your upload key or suspect it was compromised, you are not locked out and can request a reset.
sources.title: Use Play App Signing

sources.claim: An app bundle defers APK generation and signing to Google Play.
sources.title: About Android App Bundles

questions.explanation: With Play App Signing there are two keys: you sign uploads with the upload key, and Google signs what users install with the app signing key. A lost or compromised upload key can be reset. Without Play App Signing, losing the signing key can't be fixed. The upload key still authenticates your uploads, so it does matter.

questions.prompt: Version 7.2 is at a 10% staged rollout when crash rates spike. You halt the rollout. What happens next?

choices.text: Users who already installed 7.2 are automatically rolled back and silently downgraded to running version 7.1 the next time they open Play Store
Play keeps increasing the rollout percentage automatically on its own schedule unless you manually delete the entire release from the console
No additional users get 7.2; those who have it keep it, and you fix them by releasing a new build with a higher version code
Every single user who already installed 7.2 receives an automatic prompt from Play Store forcing them to reinstall the previous 7.1 build

sources.claim: When you halt a rollout, no additional users receive that version; users who already received it remain on it. If you find an issue, create and roll out a new release with a fixed app bundle. The rollout percentage won't increase automatically.
sources.title: Release app updates with staged rollouts

questions.explanation: Halting stops the rollout reaching new users but doesn't revert anyone, and Play has no downgrade path. You ship a fixed bundle as a new release with a higher version code. Rollout percentages never increase on their own.

questions.prompt: You need a critical security fix to trigger an IMMEDIATE in-app update on old versions, while normal releases only show a flexible prompt. Where does the app get the signal that a release is critical?

choices.text: From an update priority (0-5) set through the Play Developer API's `inAppUpdatePriority`, which can only be set at rollout time
From a 'priority' dropdown directly in Play Console's release page, which you can freely raise or lower at any point even after rollout
From `versionCode` jumps: internally, Play treats any jump of 100 or more between consecutive version codes as an automatically critical update
From `clientVersionStalenessDays`, a value which Play forces to exactly 0 for any release the developer has flagged as a critical update

sources.claim: Set priority with the inAppUpdatePriority field under Edits.tracks.releases in the Google Play Developer API; Play uses an integer between 0 and 5, default 0; priority can only be set when rolling out a new release and cannot be changed later.
sources.title: Support in-app updates (Kotlin or Java)

sources.claim: clientVersionStalenessDays() returns the number of days since the update became available on the Play Store.
sources.title: Support in-app updates (Kotlin or Java)

questions.explanation: Update priority is an integer from 0 (default) to 5, set only through `inAppUpdatePriority` in the Play Developer API when the release is rolled out, and it can't be changed later. The app reads it from `AppUpdateInfo` to choose IMMEDIATE or FLEXIBLE. Staleness days is the time since the update became available, not a priority, and Play Console has no priority dropdown.

questions.prompt: Design a GitHub Actions pipeline that builds, tests and lints every PR and ships a signed bundle to the internal testing track from `main`. Explain how signing keys and the Play service-account credentials are handled.

sources.claim: Secrets aren't passed to workflows triggered from forks; store small binary blobs as Base64 secrets; avoid passing secrets between processes on the command line.
sources.title: Using secrets in GitHub Actions

sources.claim: upload_to_play_store takes a track (production, beta, alpha, internal), an aab path, a json_key service-account credential, and a rollout fraction.
sources.title: upload_to_play_store - fastlane docs

questions.explanation: A senior design separates trusted from untrusted triggers and explains the two-key model, which makes a leaked CI secret recoverable. Mentioning fork-PR secret behaviour shows real operational experience.

model_answer.summary: Split into a PR workflow (build, unit tests, lint, no secrets) and a trusted release workflow on `main` that decodes the upload keystore from a Base64 secret, signs the bundle with the upload key, and uploads it with fastlane `upload_to_play_store` to the `internal` track using a service-account JSON key, with Play App Signing re-signing for users.
key_points: PR workflow (`pull_request`) runs `./gradlew` build, tests and lint with no secrets, which is safe for forks
Release workflow runs only on pushes to `main` or tags, ideally in a protected environment; the upload keystore is a Base64 secret decoded at runtime and never committed
Sign with the upload key; Play App Signing holds the app signing key, so a leaked upload key can be reset
fastlane `upload_to_play_store` with `track: internal`, `aab:` and a service-account `json_key` from a secret; internal testing reaches testers within minutes
Don't pass secrets on command lines where possible, and mask any derived sensitive values

questions.prompt: You are about to ship a risky rewrite of the checkout flow to 5 million users on Google Play. Describe your rollout plan, what you would monitor, and what you would do if something goes wrong.

sources.claim: Halting stops additional users receiving the version but users who received it remain on it; if there's an issue, roll out a new release with a fixed bundle; percentages don't increase automatically.

sources.claim: Internal testing is limited to 100 testers and bundles are available to testers within minutes; closed and open testing reach wider audiences before production.
sources.title: Set up an open, closed, or internal test

model_answer.summary: Go through internal and closed testing, then a staged production rollout at a small percentage that you raise by hand while watching crash, ANR and business metrics. A staged production rollout (for example 1% to 5% to 20% to 50% to 100%) that Play doesn't advance automatically; each step is gated on metrics
Monitor crash-free users, ANRs (Android vitals, with mapping uploaded), and checkout conversion or errors
If it goes wrong, halt: no new users receive it, but existing recipients stay, so ship a fix with a higher version code
Put the rewrite behind a remote feature flag so you can disable it without a release; use in-app update priority to push the fix

questions.prompt: A backend API change means app versions older than 6.0 will break in two weeks. How would you get users onto a supported version, and what are the limits of in-app updates?

sources.claim: For immediate updates, check for UpdateAvailability.DEVELOPER_TRIGGERED_UPDATE_IN_PROGRESS in onResume and resume the flow; if the user cancels (RESULT_CANCELED) and the app can't function, show an informative message or prompt them to close the app.
sources.title: Support in-app updates (Kotlin or Java)

sources.claim: Flexible updates download in the background; immediate updates are full-screen flows that require the user to update and restart; supported on Android 5.0 (API 21) or higher.
sources.title: In-app updates

questions.explanation: A senior answer notes that in-app updates only help versions that already contain the check, so a forced upgrade also needs a server-side version gate, and it covers the cancel path instead of assuming users comply.

model_answer.summary: Use the Play in-app updates API: ship releases with a high `inAppUpdatePriority` and have the app request IMMEDIATE updates when priority or staleness is high, resuming in-progress updates in `onResume`. key_points: IMMEDIATE is a full-screen flow that blocks use until the update installs; FLEXIBLE downloads in the background and needs `completeUpdate()` after `InstallStatus.DOWNLOADED`
Decide the flow from `updatePriority()` (0-5, set through the Play Developer API at rollout) and `clientVersionStalenessDays()`
In `onResume`, resume updates that show `DEVELOPER_TRIGGERED_UPDATE_IN_PROGRESS` so users can't escape an immediate update
If the user cancels (`RESULT_CANCELED`) and the app can't work, explain why and ask again or close the app

questions.prompt: You split a checkout feature out of a single-module app using the Now in Android layout, with `:feature:checkout:api` and `:feature:checkout:impl`. Which dependency rules keep the feature independent? Select all that apply.

choices.text: Other features' `impl` modules depend on `:feature:checkout:api`, never on its `impl`
`:feature:checkout:impl` depends on `:app` so it can reach the root navigation graph
`:core:ui` depends on `:feature:checkout:api` so shared components can open checkout
The app module depends on the feature modules and owns the UI scaffolding and navigation
Core modules such as `:core:data` never depend on feature or app modules

sources.claim: A feature's impl should only depend on another feature's api module; core modules shouldn't depend on feature nor app modules; the app module depends on all feature modules and brings together UI scaffolding and navigation.
sources.title: Now in Android: Modularization learning journey

questions.explanation: In Now in Android a feature's `impl` depends only on another feature's `api` (its navigation keys), core modules depend on neither feature nor app modules, and the app module depends on every feature and brings the navigation together. A core module depending on a feature, or a feature depending on `:app`, breaks that one-way layering and invites cycles.

questions.prompt: A teammate wants book details to open checkout by passing the whole `Book` object as a navigation argument, and to make `:feature:checkout` depend on `:feature:bookdetails` to share the `Book` class. Which changes match Android's modularization guidance? Select all that apply.

choices.text: Let the module that owns the navigation graph, usually the app module, mediate between them
Keep the feature dependency but make it `api` so both features see the same `Book` class
Put the whole serialized `Book` in the route so checkout always gets a fresh copy
Have both features depend on a shared data module that loads the book by ID
Pass the book ID as the navigation argument instead of the `Book` object

sources.claim: The mediator is the module that owns the navigation graph (usually an app module); you shouldn't pass objects as navigation arguments but simple ids that features use to load resources from the data layer, with both feature modules depending on the same data module.
sources.title: Common modularization patterns

questions.explanation: The guide says not to pass objects as navigation arguments: pass a simple ID and let each feature load the book from a shared data module, which keeps coupling low and keeps one source of truth. The mediator between two features is the module that owns the navigation graph, usually the app module. Keeping a feature-to-feature dependency (with `api` or not) is the coupling to avoid, and a serialized `Book` in the route is still an object copied out of its source of truth.

questions.prompt: Your director asks what modularizing a 200k-line single-module app will and won't deliver. Which statements match Android's modularization guide and Gradle's performance docs? Select all that apply.

choices.text: Splitting into modules speeds up builds for every project, however small its codebase
A module that keeps growing can turn into another monolith and lose the benefits
Parallel execution gives the same speedup however tightly the modules depend on each other
Very fine-grained modules add build overhead and boilerplate that can cancel out the gains
Incremental builds, the build cache and parallel builds can use module boundaries to speed up builds

sources.claim: Gradle functionalities such as incremental build, build cache or parallel build can leverage modularity to improve build performance; pitfalls are too fine-grained modules, too coarse-grained modules, and modularizing a small codebase that won't see the gains.
sources.title: Guide to Android app modularization

sources.claim: The impact of parallel builds depends on the project's structure and inter-subproject dependencies; with many dependencies between subprojects the benefits will be minimal.
sources.title: Improve the Performance of Gradle Builds

questions.explanation: Android's guide lists build time as a benefit because incremental build, build cache and parallel build can leverage modularity, and lists too fine-grained modules (overhead, boilerplate) and too coarse-grained ones (another monolith) as pitfalls. Gradle says parallel builds help little when there are many dependencies between subprojects, and Android's guide says small projects won't see the build-time gains.

questions.prompt: CI builds for a 60-module Android app are slow. Which statements about speeding them up are correct, according to the Android and Gradle docs? Select all that apply.

choices.text: Dynamic versions such as `2.+` speed up resolution because Gradle picks the newest cached match
On a hit, the configuration cache skips configuration, so build scripts and plugins aren't re-evaluated
The configuration cache also stores task outputs, so a hit skips compilation
The build cache reuses task outputs when task inputs are unchanged
Moving annotation processors from kapt to KSP helps, since kapt is significantly slower

sources.claim: The configuration cache stores the result of the configuration phase and skips re-evaluating scripts and plugins on a hit; it does not cache task outputs, which the build cache stores keyed by task inputs.
sources.title: Configuration Cache

sources.claim: kapt is significantly slower than KSP, so migrate to KSP; avoid dynamic version numbers because they cause slower builds caused by Gradle checking for updates.
sources.title: Optimize your build speed

questions.explanation: The configuration cache stores the result of the configuration phase (the task graph and its state) and skips re-evaluating scripts and plugins; it does not cache task outputs. The build cache is the one that reuses task outputs keyed by their inputs. Android's build guide recommends KSP over the much slower kapt, and says dynamic versions slow builds because Gradle checks for updates.

questions.prompt: Twenty module build scripts copy the same Android, Kotlin and Compose setup. Which statements about centralizing that build logic are correct? Select all that apply.

choices.text: Convention plugins are applied with `alias(libs.plugins...)` because the version catalog holds them
Convention plugins hold the shared setup, and each module applies them with `id(...)`
Any change to code in `buildSrc` invalidates the configuration phase and reruns all tasks
A version catalog applies the shared Android and Compose settings to every module using it
With `subprojects {}`, logic is injected into a module in a way its own build script doesn't show

sources.claim: With cross-project configuration (subprojects {}, allprojects {}), build logic can be injected into a subproject in a way that isn't obvious from its build script; changes to code in buildSrc invalidate the configuration phase and require re-execution of all tasks.
sources.title: Sharing Build Logic between Subprojects

sources.claim: Use alias for plugins that come from the version catalog file and id for plugins that don't come from the version catalog file, such as convention plugins.
sources.title: Migrate your build to version catalogs

questions.explanation: Gradle recommends convention plugins for shared configuration, and Android's catalog guide says to apply plugins that don't come from the catalog, such as convention plugins, with `id`. Gradle warns that `subprojects {}` and `allprojects {}` inject logic that isn't obvious from a module's build script, and that changing `buildSrc` invalidates configuration and reruns all tasks. A version catalog only declares versions, libraries and plugins; it applies no settings, and `alias` is for plugins it declares.

questions.prompt: An app has flavor dimensions `edition` (free, paid) and `environment` (staging, prod), plus `debug` and `release` build types. The free flavor and debug build type set `applicationIdSuffix` to `".free"` and `".debug"`; which statements are correct? Select all that apply.

choices.text: The free staging debug build's application ID ends in `.free.debug`
`androidComponents.beforeVariants` can disable unused combinations, such as release with staging
For freeStagingDebug, `src/free/` takes priority over `src/debug/`
Gradle creates 8 build variants: 2 × 2 flavors times 2 build types
The free debug build's ID ends in `.debug.free`, since build type suffixes are applied first

sources.claim: The number of build variants is the product of the number of flavors in each dimension and the number of build types; build type configuration is applied after the product flavor, giving com.example.myapp.free.debug; variants can be disabled with androidComponents.beforeVariants; source set priority is build variant, build type, product flavor, then main.
sources.title: Configure build variants

questions.explanation: The variant count is the product of the flavors in each dimension and the build types: 2 × 2 × 2 = 8. Gradle applies the build type after the flavor, so the suffixes give `.free.debug`, not `.debug.free`. `beforeVariants` with `enable = false` removes combinations nobody ships. Source set priority is build variant, then build type, then flavor, then `main`, so `src/debug/` wins over `src/free/`.

questions.prompt: After you enable R8 for release, JSON parsing through reflection crashes and a JNI call fails with `NoSuchMethodError`. Which statements are correct? Select all that apply.

choices.text: Once reflection is involved, Android's guidance is to leave R8 switched off for release builds
A package-wide `-keep class com.example.** { *; }` rule is the recommended fix
R8 can't see members looked up by name through reflection, so it may rename or remove them
R8 can't see JNI calls that find a method through a dynamic string lookup of its name
Keep rules should be as narrow as possible so R8 can still optimize the rest of the app

sources.claim: R8 can't identify classes, fields or methods accessed with reflection, or JNI calls based on a dynamic string lookup, and might rename or remove them; use keep rules that are as specific as possible.
sources.title: About keep rules

sources.claim: You should always enable optimization for your app's release build.
sources.title: Enable app optimization

questions.explanation: R8 can't identify reflective lookups such as `Class.getDeclaredMethod()` or JNI calls that rely on a dynamic string lookup, so it may rename or remove those members. The fix is keep rules that are as specific as possible, since narrowly scoped rules allow maximum optimization; a package-wide keep gives much of that up. Android says always to enable optimization for release builds.

questions.prompt: Your team wants every production crash from an R8-optimized release to be deobfuscated. Which statements are correct? Select all that apply.

A mapping file uploaded once, for the first release, also deobfuscates every version released after it

sources.title: Troubleshoot optimization

sources.claim: With an app bundle and Android Gradle plugin 4.1 or later, Play automatically grabs the deobfuscation file from the bundle; crashes before the mapping file is uploaded won't be deobfuscated, and a file is needed for each new version.
sources.title: Deobfuscate or symbolicate crash stack traces

questions.explanation: The mapping file is overwritten on every build, so a copy must be saved for each release, and `retrace` uses it to recover original stack traces. Play grabs the deobfuscation file from an app bundle automatically with AGP 4.1+. Only crashes after the upload are deobfuscated, and each new version needs its own file.

questions.prompt: Your app's download size grew 40% in a year. Which steps reduce it, according to Android's guidance? Select all that apply.

sources.title: Reduce your app size

sources.claim: If only 20% of users use a feature, making it an on-demand download reduces the initial download size for most users.

choices.text: Update priority is set per release in the Play Console's release notes field
Update priority is an integer from 0 to 5, set for a release through the Play Developer API
In-app updates are supported on every form factor, including Wear OS and Android TV

sources.title: In-app updates

questions.explanation: Immediate updates are full-screen flows that require the user to update and restart. Priority is 0 to 5, set with `inAppUpdatePriority` through the Google Play Developer API, not the Play Console. For immediate updates, check for `DEVELOPER_TRIGGERED_UPDATE_IN_PROGRESS` in `onResume` and resume the flow. They are supported only on Android 5.0 (API 21) or higher, and only on phones, tablets and ChromeOS devices, not every form factor.
